en: More important, however, is that the Constitution does not protect these legal institutions unconditionally. The phrase “having in view” performs an unequivocal finalistic function: legal protection is justified only insofar as it is oriented to the social interest and to the technological and economic development of the country. Social interest, here, is not reduced to the abstract convenience of the market nor to the private interest of the holder maximized to the limit. It designates the synthesis of the general needs of the Brazilian collectivity, measurable according to the historical, economic and social context in which protection is applied. Likewise, development is not to be confused with mere quantitative growth or rent extraction. It is a broader notion, linked to the expansion of the country's technical, social, political and economic capacities, in a manner compatible with the improvement of collective living conditions and with the material autonomy of the national community. For this reason, the patrimonial exploitation of IP finds constitutional grounding only when it remains functionally bound to this broader horizon, and not when it turns into a technique of opaque closure, relational capture and opportunistic degradation of the enjoyment already integrated into the continuous consumer relationship <1>al.</1><2>(Andrade, 2021, p. 73-81)</2>.

Hence the dogmatic consequence. Article 5, XXIX operates as a constitutional norm of conformation and limit, addressed both to the infraconstitutional legislator and to the interpreter and to those who apply the law. By saying that “the law shall ensure”, the Constitution does not merely authorize the enactment of protective norms; it conditions the very material validity of those norms and of their application on the ends it itself states. The Industrial Property Law and any other patrimonial discipline concerning industrial creations are constitutionally acceptable only to the extent that they are compatible with this finalistic frame. Outside it, what arises is not mere regulatory inconvenience, but constitutionally qualified tension. In IOC platforms, this means that exclusivity cannot be mobilized as a shield against the control of abusiveness when its concrete exercise serves to make decisions opaque, impose unilateral mutations of the experience, make minimal audit unfeasible or destroy, without restoration, the functional core of the promised enjoyment. The Constitution ensures industrial property, yes, <1>p. 705</1> but it ensures it under condition. And a constitutional condition is not rhetorical ornament; it is a criterion of validity, interpretation and containment of private power <2>al.</2><3>(Andrade, 2021, p. 109-110)</3>.

This conditioning does not act as an external, accidental or exceptional brake. Functionalization is internal to the IP regime itself. It is a form of property even more conditioned, even more socially responsible and less full than other proprietary forms, precisely because the exclusive right exists to balance private interests of exploitation and public interests of access, progress and socially useful circulation of the immaterial <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75)</2><3><4>809</4></3>. In IOC platforms, this characteristic prevents dominion over the technological or expressive infrastructure of the ecosystem from being read as authorization to organize enjoyment on bases incompatible with verifiability, trust and restoration. The power exists, but it exists functionalized.

This understanding is reinforced by the very international horizon of intellectual property. The contemporary regime does not enshrine a paradigm of metaphysically shielded exclusivity, but a balance between innovation, technological diffusion, social welfare and the distribution of rights and obligations. The protection of the holder is not an end in itself; it is legitimated precisely because it remains compatible with a broader arrangement of social reciprocity <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 662)</2><3><4>810</4></3>. In IOC platforms, the exercise of exclusivity cannot be accepted when it produces disproportionate harm to the enjoyment that has legitimately entered the consumer's sphere, above all in a context of strong technical and evidentiary asymmetry.

The social function ceases to look like a rhetorical principle and comes to function as a lock against the undue expansion of private power. It is neither a favor from the legislator nor a heteronomous intrusion upon a naturally full domain. Every subjective right is born and subsists under <1>p. 706</1> this conditioning, including intellectual rights. It makes no sense to conceive of intellectual property as an enclave in which the holder could act as he saw fit, because its legitimacy already depends, from the outset, on compatibility with social values and with other legally protected interests <2>Ascensão</2><3>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 3])</3><4><5>811</5></4>. Here, the invocation of intellectual property does not close the discussion about the manner in which power over enjoyment is exercised. It merely opens a legally more demanding discussion about its limits.

This becomes even clearer when one recalls that the exclusive intellectual right constitutes, in itself, an exception to the general freedom to use ideas and, for that very reason, must be admitted sparingly and made compatible with the collective interest. The limits of the exclusive right are neither external anomalies nor occasional concessions to the vulnerable party. They are a normal part of its conformation, a true “negation of the negation”, indispensable for keeping the channels of information, competition, culture and social communication unobstructed <1>Ascensão</1><2>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 11; p. 13; p. 14])</2><3><4>812</4></3>. The social function does not appear <5>ex post</5> to denature the effects of IP. It has always existed, always integrated it, always represented its institutional limits.

This constitutional limit acquires special relevance when the exclusivity invoked is anchored in <1>software</1>. Since the protection of the program in Brazil is not structured under a broad patent logic over function, method or result, but under a special, predominantly authorial regime, it is incompatible with the Constitution to convert technical control of the infrastructure into total power over the consumed experience. Dominion over execution, updating and modulation of the environment explains a relevant part of the platform's position, but does not authorize reading any alteration, block, sanction or suppression of enjoyment as a natural and immune consequence <2>p. 707</2> of ownership of the code. The social function operates, here, as a lock against this extrapolation. It prevents control over the technological infrastructure from being transformed into authorization to degrade enjoyment without restoration, block minimal verifiability or organize technical dependence as a form of capture of the consumer.

When supply is continuous and enjoyment depends on private infrastructure, the exercise of property and of IP ceases to be merely dominion over an asset and becomes, concretely, the power to organize consumption trajectories, expectations, reputational positions and possibilities of participation in the ecosystem. The constitutional economic order already makes this visible by subjecting property to the social function and by articulating this functionalization with consumer protection. In IOCs, this articulation means that the exercise of exclusivity cannot be dissociated from the functional integrity of supply and from the protection of the vulnerable party against the arbitrariness of whoever holds technical control of the environment. The social function of property and of the contract thus acts as a vector of rebalancing, preventing the ownership of exclusive rights from being converted into a tool of oppression, emptying of enjoyment or neutralization of the trust legitimately created in the relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 235)</2><3><4>813</4></3>.

This functionalization also acquires a concrete consumer-law feature when one observes the position of predominance exercised by the supplier that controls, at the same time, the technological asset, the architecture of the environment and the evidence of what happens in it. The vulnerability of the consumer justifies norms limiting private power precisely to prevent factual and technical superiority from turning into the material suppression of rights. In IOC platforms, this translates into duties of clarity, verifiability and preservation of functional utility, making unlawful the use of technical exclusivity to camouflage planned obsolescence, lower the quality of performance without justification or block the auditability of contractual performance <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 274)</2><3><4>814</4></3>. The social function, here, does not replace the dogmatics of the CDC. It reinforces it constitutionally.

<1>p. 708</1> The invocation of a license, industrial secret or technical prerogative is not enough, by itself, to set aside good faith, informational adequacy and control of abusiveness. In governed ecosystems, the exclusive right projects itself as a form of governance, and governance is legally attributable conduct when it affects enjoyment, access, permanence and contestation. Nor is it necessary to resort to a strong idea of the consumer's ownership of the digital good in order to demand minimal stability. That stability derives from the very structure of the consumer relationship and from the protection of legitimate expectations in continuous contracts, above all when the platform controls the conditions of intelligibility of the object and concentrates the evidence of what was altered. What is protected, then, is not a mirrored dominion of the consumer over the asset, but the functional and, where appropriate, biographical and symbolic integrity of the promised enjoyment.

It is at this point that the constructed operators appear as concretizations compatible with the social function, and not as undue aggressions against the core of exclusivity. Open auditability functions as a functional unfolding of this constitutional limit. It does not demand unrestricted opening of code, nor a broad exposure of the protected asset. It demands only that relevant alterations and sanctions with material impact be justifiable in a technically intelligible and institutionally verifiable manner, compatible with control by protection bodies and by the Judiciary. In the case of software, this is especially important, because it removes the recurring objection that any requirement of minimal transparency would amount to emptying IP itself. It does not. What the social function refuses is not the protection of the program, but the use of that protection as an absolute barrier to scrutiny of the effects of supply on the consumer's continuous enjoyment.

Functional value equivalence plays an analogous role. If exclusivity is constitutionally protected to stimulate creation and organize the market, it is fully compatible with that purpose to require that relevant updates and reconfigurations not empty the economic and existential function promised to the consumer or, when they do, that they be accompanied by adequate restoration. The social function does not freeze the ecosystem nor prevent the evolution of the service. It merely blocks the use of mutability as an instrument of extraction and normalization of losses in a context of asymmetry of information and evidence. The exclusive right may organize the market; it may not unilaterally reorganize, without control, the <1>p. 709</1> functional and symbolic content of what was acquired and enjoyed under a promise of continuity.

For this reason too, Brazilian authorial protection offers, in a subsidiary way, an interesting clue against totalizing proprietary rhetoric. The moral rights of the author are inalienable and unwaivable. This fact does not make the consumer's experience authorial, nor does it transplant the authorial moral regime into the field of the IOC. Its usefulness here is more modest and subtler. It shows that not even within authorial logic is the language of ownership reduced to pure, absolute patrimonial disposability. Within IP itself there is already internal resistance to the idea that every immaterial bond can be dissolved by a simple dispositive decision of the holder. This strengthens the refusal of the narrative according to which license, adhesion and technical control would suffice to turn governed enjoyment into a pure disposable permission.

This limit takes on a particularly sharp outline in cases of the cessation of activities, discontinuation of services or definitive shutdown of servers. As relevant portions of contemporary life migrate to private digital ecosystems, the formal precariousness of use licenses can no longer be read as automatic authorization for the complete sacrifice of immaterial objects of consumption incorporated into the consumer's trajectory. Histories, libraries, progressions, projected identities, reputational positions and long-term investments cannot be treated as residues without density merely because they are technically housed in someone else's infrastructure.

The social function of property and of intellectual property prevents exclusivity from operating as a sufficient title to legitimate the unilateral erasure of these collections under the pretext of business freedom, economic convenience or strategic reorientation of the supplier. The right to exploit, close or reorganize economic activity is not to be confused with a supposed right to annihilate, without duties of transition, preservation or transfer, the functional enjoyment already stabilized in the consumer's sphere.

If the shutdown of the service is unavoidable, the constitutional order requires that it be made compatible, as far as technically and legally possible, with solutions of continuity, portability, functional restoration, assignment of the operation or other measures suitable to prevent private architecture from becoming a lawful instrument of patrimonial and existential devastation of the consumer. Exclusivity may organize the market; it may not legitimate the administered destruction of someone else's enjoyment as a side effect of the very decision to leave it.

The social function of property and the constitutional teleology of IP oriented to social interest and development provide sufficient grounds to limit the exercise of exclusivity when it turns into opaque governance, harmful unilateral mutability or a <1>p. 710</1> technique for capturing the consumer. In IOC platforms, this limit translates into manageable criteria: a duty of verifiable justification for relevant alterations, minimal preservation of records and trails for institutional control, a requirement of restoration by functional equivalence when there is substantial loss of the core of enjoyment, and a prohibition on the use of technical dependence as a mechanism of private exclusion without a minimal standard of control. Exclusivity remains a legitimate element in the organization of the ecosystem. What it does not do is immunize its manner of exercise against consumer protection, the social function and constitutional limits on private power.

Intellectual property, as a species of the genus property at the constitutional level, does not subsist as an absolute right, being structurally bound to the realization of its social function. Each of the exclusive rights protected by the system “exists within the limits and for the functions constitutionally assigned to it”, possessing not only the social function common to all properties, but also a specific function in the design of intellectual properties, directed to the technological and economic development of the Country <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 84)</2>. It follows that exclusivity is not an end in itself, but a legal instrument conditioned by the higher objectives that justify its creation and maintenance by the State. In IOC platforms, this conditioning prevents IP ownership from being invoked as an absolute barrier against scrutiny of practices that undermine the integrity of supply and the protection of the consumer. <3>↩</3>

The legal discipline of immaterial goods is characterized by a marked functionalization, which makes it incompatible with readings that seek to isolate the holder from responsibilities toward the collectivity and users. By its very nature and mode of constitution, intellectual property is “even more functional, even more conditioned, even more socially responsible, and surely much less full than any other form of property” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 75)</2>. This intrinsic social responsibility stems from the fact that the exclusive right is a normative concession aimed at balancing private interests of exploitation and public interests of access and progress. Therefore, the exercise of technical and legal power over the platform's infrastructure does not take place in a regulatory vacuum, and must answer to the social function that legitimates the very existence of the intellectual property right. <3>↩</3>

The international regime of intellectual property reinforces the need for balance between the exclusive rights of holders and their obligations toward society, especially as regards the diffusion of knowledge and social welfare. Barbosa underlines that the TRIPs Agreement does not enshrine an absolutist paradigm, being based on a commitment to balance between the promotion of innovation and the diffusion of technology, “so as to contribute to social and economic welfare and to the balance of rights and obligations” <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2010, p. 662)</2>. This global parameter of reciprocity and responsibility confirms that the protection of exclusive rights does not authorize the exercise of power resulting in disproportionate harm to the legitimate enjoyment of end recipients, justifying the application of limits and controls aimed at preserving the functional integrity of the immaterial objects consumed. <3>↩</3>

The social function does not constitute an external or exceptional restriction imposed on the intellectual property right, but an intrinsic condition of the legitimacy of its exercise. Every subjective right, in the contemporary legal order, is born and subsists under the aegis of this ordering principle. Ascensão is emphatic in maintaining that it is “absurd to conceive of intellectual right as a right whose holder could exercise it as he saw fit”, noting that intellectual property is born subject to the principle of the social function, “like all rights” <1>Ascensão</1><2>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 3])</2>. This premise sets aside the view of IP as an enclave of private sovereignty immune to controls; on the contrary, the title of exclusivity is justified only insofar as its exercise remains compatible with social values and with the protection of others' interests equally protected by the legal system, such as the consumer's trust and the integrity of enjoyment. <3>↩</3>

The regimes of appropriation of the immaterial are limited from the origin and, for that very reason, fully compatible with external conditionings of social interest. The intellectual exclusive right does not present itself as a natural domain prior to the system, but as an exceptional technique of legal organization. Ascensão is categorical in asserting that intellectual right constitutes, in itself, “an exception to the general freedom to use ideas”, which is why its admission must be sparing and always guided by consideration of the collective interest <1>Ascensão</1><2>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 11])</2>. It follows that the limits on the exclusive right are not external anomalies, but a normal part of its own conformation. The author describes these restrictions as “the negation of the negation”, because the exclusive right itself already represents an initial restriction on common freedom; for that reason, such limits “are, for that reason, as normal as any other rules” and “are not in themselves exceptional” <3>Ascensão</3><4>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 13])</4>. The legally adequate balance, then, lies not in shielding exclusivity, but in making it compatible with the need to keep unobstructed “the channels of information, of competition, of culture”, that is, “the paths of communication and social dialogue” <5>Ascensão</5><6>(Ascensão, 2007, [p. 14])</6>. <7>↩</7>

The social function of the contract and of property acts as a vector of rebalancing in consumer relationships, preventing the ownership of exclusive rights from being turned into a tool of oppression or of hollowing out the consumer's position. In contexts of strong asymmetry, the Law uses the social function to limit the arbitrariness of whoever holds the drafting power and technical control of the object. Marques associates this principle with the pursuit of contractual justice and balance, asserting that the social function of the contract imposes limits on freedom of contract in favor of the social interest, protecting trust and objective good faith <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 235)</2>. Applied to the semiotic governance of IOCs, this guideline requires that the supplier's exercise of intellectual property override neither the integrity of the promised enjoyment nor the protection of vulnerability, since the legitimacy of exclusivity depends on its compatibility with the social and distributive purpose of the consumer contract. <3>↩</3>

The exercise of intellectual property in consumer platforms must be bounded by the social function as a limit on the private power to direct the relationship. In the consumer market, the supplier that holds technological and legal control over the immaterial object exercises a position of predominance that demands normative containment to prevent abuses. Miragem observes that the vulnerability of the consumer justifies the application of norms limiting private power, founded on the social function and on good faith, to prevent factual superiority from turning into the suppression of rights <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 274)</2>. In this sense, the social function of IP in IOC platforms imposes duties of clarity, verifiability and maintenance of functional utility, making unlawful the use of technical exclusivity to camouflage planned obsolescence, lower the quality of performance without justification or block the auditability of contractual performance. <3>↩</3>

<1>p. 680</1> Intellectual property matters here only insofar as it organizes power over enjoyment. In ecosystems of continuous digital consumption, it does not function merely as a technique for protecting creation or as an instrument of abstract economic exclusivity. It operates, in practice, as part of the legal infrastructure through which the platform defines what can be accessed, maintained, altered, withdrawn, audited and contested. The problem, therefore, is not merely knowing whether there is an exclusive right bearing on software, content, interface or related assets. It lies in understanding how this exclusivity comes to structure the consumption experience itself, conditioning continuity, intelligibility, functional equivalence and the user's real possibilities of reaction in the face of the mutability of the environment.

Intellectual property must be prevented from functioning as a theme parallel, competing or hierarchically superior to consumer protection. In continuous digital services that operate Immaterial Objects of Consumption, exclusivity does not hover above the relationship as an abstract shield of ownership. It bears on the relationship from within the supply regime, as an element of governance of the enjoyed object.

It is not enough to ask who technically controls the environment or who holds, in the abstract, the prerogative to modify the system. The legally relevant question is a different one: what limits apply when this control, founded on exclusivity, is exercised over continuous enjoyment, over expectations legitimately incorporated into the relationship and over the conditions of verifiability and contestation of the performance.

In this framework, intellectual property should be neither reduced nor demonized. Exclusivity remains legitimate and fulfills real functions of incentive, organization and protection. The point is only to refuse to read it as automatic authorization for opacity, for opportunistic mutability or for shielding against control. When exclusivity comes to operate, in the context of supply, as a technique of unilateral reconfiguration of utility, of blocking auditability, of compressing reversibility or of naturalizing opaque sanctioning regimes, it ceases to be mere protection of an asset and becomes part of the very dogmatic problem of the private governance of the IOC.

This also requires an important distinction. Not every intellectual property infrastructure offers the same type of exclusivity, nor authorizes the same claims of control. Especially in the case of software, the Brazilian discipline does not lead to an unrestricted functional sovereignty over the whole consumed experience. The legal protection of the program explains a relevant portion of the technical governance of the environment, but is not enough, by itself, to convert architecture, sanction, mutability, secrecy and the blocking of contestation into effects immune to consumer law. In IOC platforms, the exercise of exclusivity must <1>p. 681</1> remain compatible with the social function, with the protection of trust, with the functional equivalence of enjoyment and with minimal requirements of verifiable transparency.

The central question, then, is neither to revise the general theory of intellectual property nor to place it back at the center of the thesis. It is to delimit its place within the IOC regime. It appears as a structural variable of the private governance of the object, and precisely for that reason it must be read in light of the same limits that apply to that governance when it affects the adequacy, intelligibility, permanence and controllability of enjoyment. Instead of functioning as an argument for immunity, intellectual property comes to be treated as a field of compatibilization. Its exercise remains protected, but it is not separated from the constitutional order, nor does it escape the control of abusiveness, nor does it dissolve the duty of restoration when exclusivity is used as a technique for degrading the consumed experience.

With this, exclusivity ceases to appear as the final word and comes to appear as an organized legal problem. What is under examination is not the exclusive right in itself, but the way it projects onto immaterial objects of consumption whose utility depends on a governed environment. Where exclusivity serves to preserve creation and organize the ecosystem, it remains intelligible on its own terms. Where it serves structural opacity, opportunistic reconfiguration, the blocking of auditability and the capture of enjoyment under the language of license and secrecy, it must be brought back within the limits imposed by the social function, by consumer protection and by the containment of private power. It is at this point that intellectual property ceases to be a screen and becomes, itself, part of the architecture that the law needs to control.

The legal protection of continuous digital consumption demands more than the mechanical extension of consolidated categories to new realities. It demands identifying, with dogmatic precision, what kind of power operates when the enjoyment of an immaterial object depends on mutable private architecture, permanent curation and regimes of signs that organize perception, expectation and behavior. The problem no longer lets itself be satisfactorily grasped by the classical grammar of the product or the service, conceived under assumptions of stability, one-off delivery and a defect knowable by relatively direct inspection. In platform ecosystems, the experience is administered in flow, value is modulated over time and loss may arise not as an exceptional failure, but as an ordinary effect of design.

Thus, semiotic vulnerability is not to be confused with a psychological trait of the consumer, a generic synonym of digital fragility or a mere environmental description of networked life. It is a structural mechanism of power, bearing on the production of meaning, the intelligibility of the offer, the comparability between alternatives, the verifiability of enjoyment and the very conditions for contesting loss. When the architecture of the environment organizes what can be perceived, promised, inferred and proven, the asymmetry ceases to reside only in missing information and comes to operate also in the form, in the context and in the regime of visibility in which that information appears. The central question is no longer only whether something was informed, but whether it could be understood, contrasted and effectively verified in terms compatible with consumer protection.

The proposed reconstruction starts from this mutation. Instead of fitting the immaterial object of consumption into prior categories by hasty analogy, it seeks to bring back into controllable dogmatic language what is frequently naturalized as technical necessity, a rule of the system or an inevitable consequence of the infrastructure. With this, private choices of modulation, curation, opacity and sanction cease to figure as a neutral backdrop to the consumer relationship and come to be examined as a qualifiable exercise of private economic power. The constitutional order, the Consumer Protection Code and the functional limits of intellectual property together offer the criteria for this reconduction, provided they are read in light of continuous enjoyment, of the functional integrity of the object and of the centrality of the consumption environment as a space of normative incidence.

The stage now beginning thus develops a decisive shift: from the appearance of technical neutrality to the legal knowability of design; from the mere making available of <1>p. 502</1> information to the requirement of legibility and verifiability; from abusiveness understood as an isolated episode to abusiveness incorporated into the purpose of the environment. It is along this path that both the need for criteria such as open auditability and functional value equivalence and the figure of abusive teleology become visible, the latter understood as the incorporation, into the very operating logic of the object, of dynamics of inducement, extraction and normalization of losses. What is at stake is not merely correcting peripheral excesses, but delimiting, in a constitutional and consumer-law key, how far the private governance of the consumption experience may go when it comes to structure the very field of the possible for the consumer.

The application of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption depends, before anything else, on the correct qualification of what is offered to the consumer. This qualification cannot be resolved by clinging to the formal appearance of the relationship, nor by repeating the traditional categories with which the market describes its own activity. In platform ecosystems, the controversy is not adequately organized around the rigid opposition between product and service, as if it were necessary to locate, on one side, a static thing and, on the other, an instrumental activity performed from outside. The legally relevant fact lies elsewhere. What matters is to recognize situations in which the utility economically enjoyed depends structurally on an environment administered, modulated and changeable by private governance, in such a way that the consumed object only remains accessible, intelligible and functionally usable while certain conditions of infrastructure, curation, internal rule and enforcement persist.

In these cases, the qualification as an Immaterial Object of Consumption operates as the entry key to the legal regime. It is not a neutral terminological description, but a qualification with a precise dogmatic function. It shifts the focus from the civil-law ontology of the good to the continuous regime of maintenance, provision and modulation of enjoyment. What comes to matter is not the search for a stable support, autonomously inspectable and graspable outside the environment of circulation, but the identification of a bundle of immaterial utilities that is only realized under conditions continuously organized by the supplier. Enjoyment, here, does not <1>p. 718</1> appear as an accidental effect of a formally concluded contract, but as the material core of the consumer relationship.

The change of perspective is necessary because it prevents the analysis from being captured by a reifying grammar, ill-suited to objects whose use value depends less on their nominal existence than on the concrete conditions of permanence, integration and intelligibility in the ecosystem that hosts them. The consumer, in these relationships, does not enjoy a presumably stable good whose content can be isolated from the architecture that sustains it. What the consumer enjoys, rather, is a use experience continuously conditioned by technical infrastructure, access curation, update systems, visibility criteria, interaction rules and private enforcement mechanisms. In such contexts, formal ownership, a use license or the mere nominal availability of the object do not exhaust the legal problem. The central point becomes determining the conditions under which enjoyment remains possible, comprehensible and functionally preserved over time.

The consequence of this qualification is relevant on two planes. On the first, it prevents legal control from being neutralized by the supplier's descriptive strategies, especially by the claim that there is only the provision of a service or a mere content license, as if these formulas sufficed to naturalize the precariousness of the relationship and set aside the protective regime that bears on enjoyment. On the second, it redefines the axis along which the CDC is read. Instead of operating primarily from the contract as a formal statement, the discipline comes to be structured around enjoyment as a governed relationship. This does not mean denying the relevance of the contract, but refusing its explanatory sufficiency in environments in which the economic content of the relationship is realized continuously by mechanisms that go far beyond the contractual text.

Under this key, the qualification of the IOC as an immaterial product does not require denying the performance dimension of the relationship. On the contrary, it requires recognizing it in its contemporary form. What is asserted is that, whenever the consumed utility presents itself as a position of enjoyment sustained by continuous private governance, there will be an immaterial product in a legally relevant sense for the application of Article 3, paragraph 1, of the CDC. The performance does not disappear, but appears as the mode of sustaining, updating and shaping the object of consumption itself. For this reason, the old question of whether the case involves a product or a service, taken in an exclusionary key, loses much of its analytical usefulness. The problem becomes the structure of supply and the way it organizes, preserves or degrades the acquired experience.

<1>p. 719</1> This parameter thus performs the function of a trigger for the others. Without the correct qualification of the object as governed immaterial enjoyment, the subsequent parameters tend to lose adherence, because auditability, functional equivalence, abusive teleology and restoration remedies presuppose precisely the existence of a relationship in which the consumed utility depends on the continuous administration of the environment. It is this initial qualification that makes it possible to understand why alterations of rule, of access, of visibility, of integration or of performance are not mere peripheral accidents of a service external to the object, but potentially central interferences with the very experience that entered the user's sphere of consumption.

The criterion, therefore, is neither the materiality of the support nor the nomenclature employed by the supplier, but the structural dependence of enjoyment on a governed environment. Whenever this dependence proves constitutive of the acquired utility, the relationship must be read as a case of an Immaterial Object of Consumption, with all the dogmatic consequences deriving from it. This makes it possible to abandon the false security of watertight classifications and to recognize that, in platform economies, the core of the conflict lies less in the possession of a good or in the isolated performance of a service than in the legal discipline of an enjoyment maintained, modulated and potentially made precarious by private architecture. It is on this plane that the CDC regains its explanatory and corrective force.

The legal response to conflicts involving the Immaterial Object of Consumption cannot be organized around the traditional automatism of converting the injury into pecuniary compensation. This solution, although often necessary, frequently proves insufficient when what is at stake is not only the immediate economic loss, but the degradation, interruption or abusive reconfiguration of a continuous enjoyment that is governed and functionally situated within an ecosystem. In relationships of this nature, the mere later payment of a sum of money may leave the harmful mechanism untouched, preserve the architecture that produced the problem and normalize the repetition of the loss as an ordinary cost of the supply model. For this reason, the discipline of remedies must start from another premise. Priority protection, whenever technically and legally feasible, must seek the functional restoration of enjoyment and the correction of the regime that rendered it inadequate.

This primacy does not derive from an abstract preference for specific relief nor from a ritual attachment to the idea of restoration in natura. It derives from the very structure of the relationship. If the consumed utility presents itself as an immaterial experience maintained by continuous governance, the relevant injury tends to bear on access, continuity, integrity, equivalence, intelligibility, history, relational position or the consumer's meaningful insertion in the environment. In these cases, the automatic monetization of the conflict frequently fails to give back what was <1>p. 740</1> actually compromised. Money may roughly compensate certain economic losses, but it does not always restore the practical utility, the functional position or the relational and symbolic dimension of enjoyment. Functional restoration takes on centrality because it corresponds more adequately to the nature of the legal interest affected.

This becomes even more evident in immaterial objects of consumption endowed with high identity, historical or reputational density. In such cases, the value of enjoyment is not limited to the acquisition cost of an item, an account or a feature. It may be linked to a trajectory of use, accumulated history, belonging to a community, recognition within the ecosystem, relational insertion and meaningful continuity of the experience. When these elements are affected, protection that simply sets a pecuniary sum runs the risk of treating as equivalent what, in practice, is not. Functional and symbolic restoration then becomes not only a more protective alternative, but a form more legally faithful to the content of the injury.

This parameter thus performs the function of closing the regime. Once the object is recognized, the vulnerability identified, the duties of information and advertising controlled, auditability required, functional equivalence measured, any abusive teleology ascertained and evidence organized in an environment of structural opacity, the decisive question arises as to what to do with the conflict. The answer cannot be neutral with regard to the architecture of the injury. When the problem stems from continuous, repeatable and structural governance, protection must also be conceived in a functional and structural key. This requires going beyond later compensation and considering remedies capable of restoring the experience, interrupting the reiteration of the harmful mechanism and correcting the mode of operation that made the injury ordinary.

Functional restoration, in this context, comprises a set of possible measures, calibrated according to the structure of the compromised enjoyment. It may involve maintenance or restoration of access, reversal or review of sanctions, preservation of history, reactivation of features, substitution by a functionally equivalent position, reversibility of versions when technically possible, procedural corrections of governance, duties of verifiable reasoning, intelligible mechanisms of contestation and other means apt to re-establish, substantially, the utility legitimately incorporated into the relationship. The criterion is not the literal reproduction of the prior state at any cost, but the functionally adequate restitution of the injured experience, at a level compatible with what the consumer had legitimately incorporated into their sphere of enjoyment.

This point is important because it prevents two undue reductions. The first is to treat all specific relief as impracticable merely because the environment is technically complex <1>p. 741</1> or continuously changing. Complexity is not the same as impossibility. The second is to assume that any restoration would be excessively intrusive upon business freedom. Here too the reasoning needs to be more sober. What is required is neither the freezing of the ecosystem nor the submission of every technical decision of the supplier to the individual will of the consumer. All that is required is that, in the face of a relevant injury to governed enjoyment, the legal response not automatically settle for residual monetization when there are reasonable means of restoring access, functionality, position of use or minimal conditions of intelligibility and contestation. In other words, the architecture of the environment cannot serve as an automatic excuse for downgrading remedies.

The primacy of functional restoration takes on even greater importance when the injury is architectural, repeatable and incorporated into the ordinary regime of supply. In these cases, merely compensatory individual protection tends to operate as a manageable cost of the business model, without altering the structure that produces the harm. The problem then ceases to be only the loss suffered by a specific consumer and comes to lie in the persistence of a harmful arrangement capable of reproducing the same inadequacy indefinitely. The parameter, for this reason, makes room for regime correction. This means admitting, when the case reveals a structural pattern of abusiveness, remedies aimed at the reconfiguration of flows, the imposition of procedural duties, the review of sanction mechanisms, the requirement of verifiable reasoning, the creation of intelligible channels of contestation and other measures apt to reach the continuous source of the problem.

This opening is particularly relevant because it reconnects individual protection to the collective and institutional dimension of the IOC regime. In many platform conflicts, the harmful experience of the individual consumer is only a localized manifestation of a broader form of inadequate governance. Treating the case exclusively as an isolated event means losing sight of the repeatability of the harm and of the environment's capacity to produce the same injury serially. Regime correction, by contrast, makes it possible to treat the harm as architectural and not merely as an episode. This makes it possible to justify injunctive relief, structural measures, collective measures and even mechanisms of compulsory compliance compatible with open auditability and institutional control of enjoyment. The legal response then comes to act not only on the consequences of the model, but on its mode of operation.

Pecuniary compensation remains, of course, a legitimate and in many cases indispensable remedy. The parameter formulated here does not eliminate it. It merely returns it to a systematically more precise position. It takes on a residual or complementary nature whenever functional restoration is unfeasible, insufficient or incapable of fully covering the <1>p. 742</1> losses suffered. In these cases, monetary compensation continues to play an important role, whether to make good material losses or to recognize non-pecuniary damages when present. What is rejected is its transformation into an automatic and preferential response in every case, as if the injury to the IOC could always be adequately translated into a figure without regard for the structure of the compromised enjoyment.

The parameter, therefore, affirms a remedial orientation consistent with the whole preceding path. If the relationship is one of governed enjoyment, the remedy must aim at enjoyment. If the injury is structural, protection must reach the structure. If the loss is functional, the priority response must be functionally restorative. Only thus does the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption avoid being reduced to a sophisticated grammar of diagnosis without real transformative force. The primacy of functional restoration and regime correction prevents consumer protection from limiting itself to pricing harms while leaving intact the machine that produces them. Turning structural abuses into mere operating expenses is, in practice, to neutralize the Law by way of accounting.

The vulnerability relevant to the application of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption cannot be understood as a generic attribute of the digital, nor be reduced to economic hyposufficiency or to the consumer's lesser individual ability to understand technically complex environments. This reading is insufficient because it shifts the problem onto the person of the user and obscures the power structure that shapes the relationship. What is decisive is to recognize that, in platform-governed ecosystems, expectation, consent, perception of value, perception of risk and the possibility of contestation depend on signs, interfaces, informational flows and experience trails controlled by the supplier itself. Vulnerability, in this context, emerges as a structural effect of the way the environment organizes meaning.

That is why the vulnerability relevant here must be qualified as semiotic vulnerability. The term does not designate naivety, credulity or cultural deficiency of the consumer. It designates a mechanism of power inscribed in the architecture of <1>p. 720</1> supply, through which the supplier administers the modes of presentation of the object, the criteria of visibility of relevant information, the routes of comprehension of the experience, the perceived equivalences and the practical possibilities of resistance or reaction. Instead of operating only on conscious and one-off choices, this form of power bears on the very intelligibility of the relationship, conditioning how the object is perceived, how its promise is decoded and how its later alteration may or may not be recognized as legally relevant.

This qualification is important because it prevents the analysis from falling into moralism about the consumer's conduct. It is not a matter of asking whether the user was sufficiently attentive, distrustful or technically informed. Nor is it a matter of presupposing absolute incapacity in the face of the digital. The question is objective. Whenever the consumption experience is mediated by signs and interfaces whose design, hierarchy, salience and mutability are controlled by the supplier, there will be a field of semiotic asymmetry potentially relevant to the Law. The consumer depends, in these cases, on an environment whose vocabulary, rhythm, emphases and criteria of legibility are not neutral. They are produced, selected and reorganized by whoever holds the power of governance of the ecosystem.

What is distinctive about this mechanism is that the asymmetry of meaning tends to be accompanied by an asymmetry of evidence. Whoever controls the way the object is made intelligible frequently also controls the records by which that intelligibility can be reconstructed in case of conflict. Logs, interface histories, screen versions, curation criteria, alteration records, visibility parameters and decision traces remain under the supplier's control. The result is a double concentration of power. On one side, the capacity to shape the ordinary reading of enjoyment is concentrated. On the other, the capacity to narrate retrospectively, in institutionally acceptable terms, what occurred in the relationship is concentrated. In environments of this nature, semiotic vulnerability is not an accidental layer of the relationship. It is a recurring part of the way it operates.

This finding has a relevant dogmatic consequence. Semiotic vulnerability does not operate only as a sociological description of the environment, but as a category of attribution and control. Its usefulness lies in tracing duties, burdens and legal limits back to the concrete structure of the governance of meaning. It makes it possible to understand why the duty to inform, in these contexts, is not satisfied by textual volume; why advertising must be read as management of expectation and not only as a promotional statement; why evidence cannot be organized while ignoring the private concentration of records; and why the very <1>p. 721</1> mutability of the environment can convert seemingly minor alterations into legally relevant forms of capture, obscuring or displacement of enjoyment.

The parameter also has a delimiting function. It prevents every difficulty experienced in a digital environment from being automatically converted into legally qualified vulnerability. It is not enough that the case involves an interface, an algorithm or an online environment. It is necessary that the governance of meaning act structurally on the comprehension, comparability, predictability or contestation of enjoyment. What is controlled, therefore, is not the mere existence of technological mediation, but the configuration of an arrangement in which signs, paths and records are asymmetrically organized by whoever also holds the power of alteration, sanction or modulation of the relationship. Semiotic vulnerability gains legal relevance precisely when it becomes an objective condition of the consumer relationship and interferes with the institutional legibility of the conflict.

Read this way, the category rules out two equally inadequate reductionisms. The first reduces vulnerability to informational poverty in a quantitative sense, as if it sufficed to measure how much the consumer knew or failed to know. The second dissolves it into a cultural abstraction about the “digital society”, losing sight of the concrete mechanisms by which the relationship is organized. The parameter proposed here refuses both. Semiotic vulnerability is relational, structural and functional. Relational, because it arises from the position the parties occupy in the production and administration of meaning. Structural, because it stems from the design of the environment and not only from isolated episodes. Functional, because it only acquires dogmatic relevance when it interferes with the formation of expectation, the reading of utility, the assessment of risk or the consumer's possibility of institutional reaction.

With this formulation, the application of the IOC regime keeps its focus on the contemporary exercise of private power in consumption. The center of the analysis is no longer a supposed personal insufficiency of the user but the governance of meaning as a technology for organizing enjoyment. This avoids both the romanticization of consumer autonomy in structurally asymmetric environments and the abstract infantilization of the consumer's legal position. What is asserted is more precise. On platforms that control signs, flows, records and criteria of legibility, vulnerability takes a semiotic form because it is through it that private power administers perception, predictability and contestation. Recognizing it as a mechanism is a condition for legal protection to bear on the real structure of the relationship, and not on moral caricatures of its participants.

In platform ecosystems, the duty to inform cannot be understood in merely quantitative terms. The mere accumulation of texts, <1>links</1>, notices, policies, terms and explanatory windows does not, by itself, satisfy the requirement of adequate information. In many cases, this accumulation works precisely in the opposite direction, producing an environment of merely apparent transparency, in which the proliferation of statements takes the place of the legibility of what actually matters for deciding, adhering, remaining or contesting. Informational inadequacy, in this context, does not necessarily stem from the material absence of information. It may result from the way information is organized, fragmented, hierarchized, distributed over time and made accessible under conditions that prevent its practical usefulness.

Compliance with the duty to inform cannot be reduced to a bureaucratic logic of textual deposit. To inform is not merely to make content available. To inform, in a legally relevant sense, is to make intelligible the essential elements of enjoyment at the moment the consumer's decision is formed and, at the same time, to preserve minimal conditions for the later reconstruction of what was promised, what was shown and what was altered. Adequate information, therefore, is not measured by the volume of what was published, but by its aptitude to guide conduct and allow institutional verification. Where excess replaces clarity, noise replaces comprehension and apparent abundance conceals the essential, the duty remains violated.

The transformation of this duty on platforms is particularly important because the environment of continuous consumption tends to operate through multiple communicational layers. The consumer does not encounter only a centralized and stable contractual text. He faces successive interface flows, scattered notices, secondary menus, help centers, versioned policies, partial explanations, promotional communications, contextual notifications and later alterations that redraw the informational field without offering a material synthesis of what changed. In this architecture, opacity may be produced not by outright omission, but by the strategic distribution of information along discontinuous trails of low salience or difficult reconstruction. What presents itself as communicational diligence may, in truth, function as a technique of obscuring.

Informational inadequacy may thus take the form of excess, dispersion and flow architecture. Excess, when textual overload makes it impracticable to distinguish the essential from the accessory. Dispersion, when the relevant elements of the relationship are scattered across multiple documents, screens and paths without sufficient integration. Flow architecture, <1>p. 723</1> when the informational experience is designed to enhance the attractive, simplify the favorable and push the onerous, the contingent or the restrictive into zones of low visibility, lesser salience or improbable reading. In these cases, the violation of the duty cannot be adequately described as a simple lack of information. It is functional opacity produced by design, that is, a specific form of informational non-performance in which the appearance of openness replaces the actual legibility of the regime of enjoyment.

This parameter is particularly useful because it shifts the discussion from the abstract existence of information to its usefulness for decision and its institutional verifiability. The legally relevant question is no longer whether a given piece of data was somewhere in the supplier's documentary ecosystem. It becomes whether that data was made accessible, comprehensible and relevant at the moment it could influence the legitimate formation of expectation or the consumer's reaction. Likewise, in case of later controversy, what matters is whether the informational arrangement preserves minimal trails that make it possible to reconstruct the link between offer, presentation of the environment, modulation of enjoyment and alteration of the content of the relationship. Without this possibility of reconstruction, information fails not only to guide choice, but also to allow institutional control of the conflict itself.

The centrality of verifiable adequacy also prevents the supplier's standard defense from resting on the claim that “everything was in the contract”. This formula confuses formal existence with material compliance with the duty. In environments of high informational complexity, the contract may even contain a nominal reference to the disputed risk, alteration or limitation, and still fail to inform adequately if the organization of the communicational whole produces noise, minimizes the impact of the relevant data or makes their practical connection with the consumer's decision unfeasible. The duty to inform does not protect only against direct factual lies. It also protects against the strategic displacement of what is legally relevant to regions of low intelligibility.

This formulation carries an important consequence for immaterial objects of consumption of high cognitive complexity, including those in which the very utility of the object involves guidance, filtering, prioritization or informational support. In these contexts, breach of the duty may occur without any literal falsehood and without any absolute silence. It suffices that the communicational architecture replace comprehension with an impression of completeness, or that textual delivery function as a misleading substitute for legibility. The problem then ceases to be the presence or absence of isolated data and comes to lie in the relation between promise, mode of presentation, real conditions of use and the institutional possibility of auditing the informational trajectory of the relationship.

<1>p. 724</1> The parameter, therefore, demands a material reading of the duty to inform. Informational adequacy must be measured by the capacity of the communicational arrangement to make visible and comprehensible the elements that relevantly condition the formation of expectation, the preservation of enjoyment and the possibility of contestation. Where there is excess without guidance, abundance without hierarchy, documentation without legibility or transparency without reconstructability, there will be no true performance of the duty. There will be, rather, a sophisticated form of functional opacity, incompatible with the consumer-law discipline of an environment in which enjoyment depends on continuous governance and in which private power is also exercised through the administration of what can be known, perceived and proven.

In ecosystems in which enjoyment is preceded, prepared and guided by continuous cycles of anticipation, advertising and offer cannot be treated as an external, ornamental or legally neutral layer of consumption. In many immaterial objects of consumption, what is acquired is not only a statically described functional utility, but an experience framed in advance by signs, promises, narratives of distinction, projections of value and expectations administered by the supplier itself. The offer, in these cases, is not limited to the final purchase statement. It is built progressively through an economy of signals that precedes enjoyment, organizes its horizon of meaning and conditions the way the consumer interprets what is being acquired.

This particularity demands a material reading of advertising. Teasers, showcases, promotional events, announcement cycles, previews, countdowns, suggestions of rarity, insinuated equivalences, promises of prestige, belonging or performance and narrative models of scarcity do not operate, in these environments, as mere accessory persuasion. They make up the offer program insofar as they take part in the formation of legitimate expectation and in the determination of the value attributed to the object. What is presented to the consumer is not merely a piece of content or an isolated feature, but an experience of enjoyment shaped in advance by a carefully curated regime of signs. For this reason, the legal analysis of the offer cannot remain restricted to the most immediate literal statement, as if the relevant promise were exhausted in a sentence formally detached from the rest of the communicational environment.

This perspective makes it possible to recognize forms of misleadingness that cannot be captured solely by the classical logic of outright falsehood. In immaterial objects of consumption, inducement <1>p. 725</1> into error may result from constructed ambiguity, from strategically distributed relevant omission or from a mismatch between the overall meaning of the promise and the real conditions of enjoyment under administered mutability. Advertising may suggest stability where there is structural precariousness, equivalence where there is relevant asymmetry, rarity where there is programmed artificiality, freedom of use where there is asymmetric reversibility, continuity where there is intense mutability. In these cases, the nonconformity lies not only in an isolated factual lie, but in the management of meaning by which the supplier produces a favorable reading of the object and shifts the cognitive costs of actual comprehension onto the consumer.

Hypercuratorial anticipation is thus part of the very legal economy of the offer. When the supplier administers cycles of expectation, projects models of value and structures the visibility of what will be perceived as central or secondary in the acquisition, it is not merely announcing something that will exist later. It is taking part in the very shaping of the economically enjoyed object. This becomes even more evident in environments in which the utility consumed has a relevant symbolic, relational or reputational dimension. In such cases, use value and meaning value intertwine. The consumer acquires not only access or functionality, but also a place in a network of distinction, recognition, belonging or identity projection modeled in advance by the supplier's communication. Advertising, in this context, is no longer a mere external discourse about the object and becomes a material part of its regime of enjoyment.

The dogmatic consequence is clear. Control of the offer must bear on what was promised as value and as function, on what was concealed as cost, limitation or condition of precariousness, and on the correspondence between this semiotic frame and the real enjoyment made available to the consumer. This requires understanding advertising as controllable management of meaning. It is not a matter of denying the persuasive function proper to economic activity, but of recognizing that, in platform-governed ecosystems, persuasion may turn into a technique of structural shaping of expectation and, for that reason, must be subjected to the limits of the consumer-law regime. Whenever promotional communication takes part in determining what the consumer legitimately understands he is acquiring, it is incorporated into the normative field of the offer and becomes susceptible to control for misleadingness, ambiguity or relevant omission.

This parameter also prevents the examination of advertising from being reduced to the isolated reading of sentences or individual pieces. The legally relevant promise is not always concentrated in a single statement. It frequently emerges from the articulation between multiple elements of the communicational environment, some explicit, others insinuated, still others <1>p. 726</1> merely suggested by salience, timing, symbolic association or strategic repetition. Control must, for this reason, capture the overall regime of signification produced by the supplier. This requirement is particularly important in immaterial objects of consumption whose enjoyment depends on visibility, reputation, collective recognition or insertion in an ecosystem of symbolic value. In them, the mismatch between promise and delivery may not appear as an evident technical defect, but as a relevant frustration of the symbolic or relational position presented as part of the core of the acquisition.

For this reason too, advertising takes on a function of semiotic hygiene of the offer. The expression is important because it shifts the debate from the simplistic idea of advertising as an inevitably exaggerated adornment to a more demanding understanding of the consumption environment. When communication is designed to produce ambiguity, artificially enhance the favorable, obscure the onerous or push the essential into zones of low visibility, it ceases to be a mere persuasive frame and becomes part of the supply program itself. In this condition, it may take part not only in the formation of inadequate expectation, but in the very abusive teleology of the ecosystem, above all when it is combined with later mechanisms of mutability, artificial scarcity, manufactured urgency or deliberate opacity.

The parameter, therefore, requires that offer and advertising be read in light of their concrete function in the governance of enjoyment. What matters is not only what was formally said, but what was legally promised through the management of signs, expectations and saliences. Where prior communication relevantly shapes the reading of the object, forms part of the perception of its value and conditions the consumer's adhesion, there will be an offer in a materially controllable sense. And where this management of meaning operates to produce relevant ambiguity, shift cognitive costs, conceal precariousness or artificially inflate perceived utility, there will be sufficient grounds for the application of the protective regime, not as abstract repression of advertising, but as control of the promise in environments of governed enjoyment.

The controllability of the Immaterial Object of Consumption requires that relevant alterations of the service, of access, of the conditions of enjoyment and of the very objects incorporated into the ecosystem can be institutionally reconstructed in case of controversy. This requirement does not stem from technical curiosity about the internal workings of the platform, nor from a maximalist claim to full transparency. It stems from the elementary need to prevent the <1>p. 727</1> structural opacity of the environment from operating as a mechanism of practical immunization against legal control. Whenever enjoyment depends on continuous private governance, the discipline of the relationship presupposes some degree of verifiable intelligibility about what was altered, when, for what reasons it was justified and what relevant effects it produced on the consumer's experience.

It is in this context that open auditability is asserted as a parameter of legitimacy. The expression does not designate unrestricted opening of source code, full exposure of the technological architecture or a generalized waiver of business secrets. Its core is more precise and institutionally more defensible. Open auditability means the existence of minimal conditions of verifiability about relevant aspects of supply, so that protection bodies, the Judiciary, experts and, to a certain extent, consumers themselves can reconstruct the relation between promise, alteration, sanction, functional impact and the justification presented by the supplier. What is demanded is not to strip the whole system bare, but to make controllable, at a sufficient level, whatever legally interferes with enjoyment.

This parameter breaks down a false dichotomy that often contaminates the debate. On one side, it is argued that any requirement of transparency would compromise industrial secrecy, innovation or business autonomy. On the other, it is assumed that control would only be effective if the platform's internal workings were fully opened. Both positions are bad. The first turns technical complexity into an alibi for irresponsibility. The second confuses legal protection with total invasion of the productive environment. Open auditability rejects this binary theater. It starts from the premise that exclusivity, complexity and secrecy can coexist with minimal duties of institutional intelligibility, provided these bear on the elements relevant to understanding the conflict and to reconstructing the disputed supply.

The requirement is therefore selective and functional. What must be auditable is not everything, but what matters to make the controversy decidable. Relevant alterations of access rules, reconfigurations with functional impact, version changes that affect utility or performance, sanctions bearing on permanence or visibility, ordinary modulations of the environment and decision criteria with material repercussions on enjoyment cannot remain in a zone of undemonstrability shielded by the mere claim of technicality. In these cases, the platform must be able to preserve and exhibit trails, records, minimal logs, operational justifications and contextualizing elements sufficient to allow bounded institutional verification. It is not a matter of demanding a self-congratulatory narrative from the supplier, but of imposing objective conditions for control.

<1>p. 728</1> This point is especially important because, in platform-governed ecosystems, opacity does not function only as a technical characteristic of the environment. It functions as an asymmetric distribution of power within the relationship. Whoever controls the criteria of alteration, the records of what was done, the memory of the system and the language in which these events can be described also concentrates the capacity to define what will be considered demonstrable. Without minimal auditability, the conflict tends to be degraded into an unequal confrontation between the consumer's subjective experience and a formally self-justified corporate version. Private governance then ceases to be only a power to modulate enjoyment and becomes also a power to control the institutional conditions of evidence. It is precisely against this practical immunity that the parameter is directed.

Open auditability also performs a function of containing litigation. Paradoxically, contrary to what is often claimed, the minimum of institutional verifiability does not indefinitely expand technical judicialization. It rationalizes it. When there are preserved trails, identifiable relevant versions, minimally statable reasons for alteration and basic elements for reconstructing the conflict, the judicial discussion is prevented from turning into an endless war of opaque technicalities, in which each side speaks a different language and the decision ends up handed over to intuitive deference to the more organized party. The parameter does not seek to hypercomplexify the proceedings. It seeks to create sufficient grounding for the controversy to be delimited and for expert examinations, document production and orders for clarification to bear on knowable objects, and not on self-immune corporate abstractions.

The intelligibility required by this parameter does not coincide with absolute explainability. Law does not need to understand, in their microscopic totality, all the internal flows of the system in order to exercise legitimate control over the consumer relationship. What it needs is sufficient intelligibility to identify the occurrence of a relevant alteration, relate it to the promised enjoyment, verify whether there was a justification compatible with the legal regime and ascertain whether the sanction, the change or the modulation respected minimal standards of predictability, proportionality and contestability. The parameter is calibrated precisely to make control possible without demanding technical omniscience from the judge or disrupting the economic operation of the ecosystem. In governed environments, this is what separates legitimate complexity from obscurity turned into a technique of power. Not total transparency, but sufficient transparency. Not absolute revelation, but minimal verifiability. Not a sweeping search of the system, but refusal of the practical immunity produced by structural opacity.

This formulation has a relevant consequence for the application of the CDC in platform environments. Business secrecy, economic exclusivity and the complexity of the <1>p. 729</1> service cease to operate as absolute vetoes on control and become elements to be reconciled with duties of minimal verifiability. The platform remains the holder of its intangible assets and its internal architecture, but can no longer invoke them to prevent entirely the institutional reconstruction of events that affect the consumer's enjoyment in a legally relevant way. Structural opacity thus ceases to be a zone naturally immune to protection and becomes a legal problem that can be addressed through preservation orders, bounded document production, restricted expert examination, verifiable reasoning and other instruments compatible with the procedural and administrative rationality of the protective system.
