The legal legitimacy of mutability in platform ecosystems cannot be assessed on the basis of the mere nominal continuity of the object, nor by the simple finding that the digital environment, by its nature, admits ordinary updates, adjustments and reconfigurations. Mutability, by itself, is not unlawful. The problem begins when it ceases to operate as a legitimate form of maintaining, improving or adapting the supply and comes to degrade, empty or divert, to a relevant degree, the function that justified the acquisition and structured the legitimate expectation of enjoyment. It is at this point that functional value equivalence emerges as a central parameter of control. Its usefulness lies in providing a criterion capable of distinguishing change compatible with the continuity of the relationship from alteration that converts the plasticity of the environment into a technology of normalized loss.

Functional value equivalence cannot be reduced to maintaining technical performance in the strict sense, nor to the quantitative preservation of isolated attributes. Its content is more demanding. What matters is the substantial preservation of the role the object plays in the acquired experience, considering its concrete utility in the ecosystem, its relational place in the environment of use and, when legally relevant, its identity or symbolic density. In immaterial objects of consumption, functional value does not necessarily coincide with operational efficiency measurable by linear indicators. It is often also constituted by the position the object occupies in the consumer's trajectory of enjoyment, by the type of interaction it allows, by the way it connects with other parts of the ecosystem and by the practical meaning it takes on in the acquired experience.

Legal control of mutability must not be held prisoner by an excessively formal or technicist logic. Relevant alterations may keep the name, general appearance or nominal existence of the object and still substantially compromise the <1>p. 730</1> enjoyment legitimately incorporated into the relationship. The permanence of the item, the functionality, the account, the access or the feature does not, by itself, neutralize the emptying of the experience if the concrete role of the object is degraded, diverted or made substantially different from the one that justified the acquisition. Functional equivalence works precisely against this kind of defense. It prevents the supplier from relying on apparent continuity to conceal a relevant loss of practical content.

From this perspective, legally legitimate mutability is that which substantially preserves the function of the object in the consumer's experience. This does not mean demanding perfect identity between the earlier and later versions, nor imposing a freeze on the service. Continuous digital environments presuppose evolution, adaptation and, in many cases, internal rebalancing. What the parameter rejects is not change in itself, but its use as an instrument to shift onto the consumer the cost of reconfigurations that destroy or significantly lower the acquired utility without compatible restoration. Equivalence, therefore, does not demand formal equality of attributes. It demands preservation of the functional role of the object in the ecosystem of enjoyment, so that the alteration does not become a technique for extracting or normalizing losses.

This formulation is especially suited to controlling ordinary reconfigurations presented as unavoidable technical routine. Nerfs, removals, reworks, migrations, rule changes, reordering of access, reconfiguration of interfaces and suppression of features are usually narrated as the natural evolution of the environment. In many cases, they may indeed be so. The parameter of functional equivalence is precisely what makes it possible to separate legitimate mutation from degrading mutation. The legally relevant question then ceases to be whether the change occurred within the supplier's general power to update. It becomes whether, after the alteration, the acquired experience remains substantially functionally equivalent to the one that legitimated the entry of the object into the user's sphere of consumption.

This shift has an important dogmatic consequence. It means that the core of the conflict is resolved not by abstract reference to the business autonomy to manage the ecosystem, but by concretely assessing whether enjoyment has been preserved. The analysis must address the impact of the alteration on the role played by the object, on the relational performance of its utility, on its meaningful place in the environment and, when the case requires, on its identity or symbolic dimension. In some ecosystems, the value of the object lies not only in its instrumental efficacy, but also in its form of recognition, visibility, belonging or projection within the experience of use. In these cases, functional equivalence <1>p. 731</1> may also require preservation of the relational and symbolic density of enjoyment, provided this dimension forms, in an objectively recognizable way, the core of the acquisition.

The parameter thus prevents two opposite distortions. On one side, it sets aside the claim to freeze the environment in a fixed state, as if any mutation automatically constituted non-performance. On the other, it refuses the thesis that every alteration would be legitimated by the simple operational continuity of the system or by the mere nominal survival of the object. Between these extremes, functional equivalence offers an intermediate and institutionally more useful yardstick. It makes it possible to recognize that mutability is compatible with continuous supply, but only as long as it does not destroy the core of enjoyment that gave economic and legal meaning to the acquisition.

This yardstick also structures the legal response to the conflict. When equivalence is broken without adequate restoration, the alteration ceases to be read as ordinary evolution and comes to be treated as a relevant inadequacy of the supply regime. Room then opens for protection aimed not only at residual economic compensation, but at restoring enjoyment in functionally equivalent terms. That is precisely where the centrality of this parameter lies. It serves not only to identify unlawfulness. It also serves to guide remedies. By shifting the focus to the functional core of the acquired experience, it makes it possible to prioritize restoration, equivalent substitution, technical reversal when feasible or other forms of restoration that preserve the practical meaning of the relationship, instead of automatically reducing the injury to later monetization.

Functional value equivalence, therefore, constitutes the material core of the control of mutability in immaterial objects of consumption. Its function is to ensure that the plasticity of digital environments is not turned into a license to empty out, from within, what was economically incorporated into the consumer's experience. Where the alteration substantially preserves the function of the object, there will be legitimate mutability. Where the change relevantly degrades the functional, relational or symbolically constitutive role of enjoyment without compatible restoration, there will be legally controllable inadequacy. It is at this point that the IOC regime proves capable of treating mutation not as a brute fact of technology, but as conduct subject to limits, evidence and normative consequence.

The controllability of the Immaterial Object of Consumption requires recognizing that not all relevant abusiveness manifests itself in the classical form of an isolated clause, a singular event or a <1>p. 732</1> one-off failure of performance. In platform-governed ecosystems, there are cases in which exploitation does not stem from an episodic deviation of the system, but from the very operating program that organizes enjoyment. In these cases, the injury cannot be adequately grasped by decomposing the conflict into autonomous incidents, because it is precisely the coordination between multiple elements of the environment that makes its exploitative purpose knowable. When inducement, extraction and normalization of losses are stably incorporated into the design of the ecosystem, the problem ceases to be merely one of fragmentary non-performance and comes to constitute a teleological unlawful act of architecture.

Abusive teleology thus describes a situation in which the practical purpose of the supply arrangement departs from legally tolerable limits and comes to direct the environment toward the structural exploitation of vulnerability, toward the relevant obscuring of enjoyment or toward the recurring conversion of mutability into a technology of capture. It is not a matter of investigating the subjective psychological intention of business agents, nor of moralizing every form of monetization, persuasion or private governance. The focus lies on the functional purpose objectively inscribed in the arrangement, as revealed by its replicability, its internal coherence and its repeated impact on the consumer's experience. What is controlled is not an inner will, but a recognizable operating program.

This formulation is important because it prevents two impoverishing reductions. The first consists in dispersing the conflict into apparently modest micro-events, each of which is insufficient, in isolation, to reveal the gravity of the pattern. The second consists in turning the critique of architecture into an abstract moral judgment against business activity, losing institutional traction. The parameter of abusive teleology avoids both extremes. It makes it possible to identify cases in which micro-frictions, micro-losses, micro-opacities, discreet shifts of information, asymmetric reversibilities, manufactured urgencies, artificial scarcities, elastic equivalences and selective regimes of difficulty operate in a coordinated manner, forming a program of extraction that, seen as a whole, becomes legally relevant. Taken in isolation, such elements may seem merely tolerable rough edges of the environment. Structurally articulated, they reveal a mode of governance oriented toward the ordinary exploitation of enjoyment.

The core of the parameter lies in treating architecture as conduct. As long as the design of the environment is perceived only as a neutral technical setting, it will remain outside the main field of legal attribution. Conversely, once it is recognized that architecture organizes access, visibility, timing, friction, irreversibility, contestation, salience and modulation of the experience, it becomes possible to understand it as the supplier's way of acting. The platform <1>p. 733</1> no longer appears only as the abstract holder of infrastructure or as the drafter of contractual documents. It appears as an agent that shapes, by design, the material conditions in which choice occurs, loss is normalized, reaction is hindered and extraction is stabilized. It is in this sense that the teleological unlawful act of architecture can be qualified as legally attributable conduct.

The category also prevents technical necessities from being accepted, automatically, as self-evident justifications for any arrangement of enjoyment. Technique, in environments of this nature, is not external to power. It is one of its privileged forms of exercise. For this reason, claims of efficiency, optimization, balance of the system, operational convenience or the need for updating are not enough, by themselves, to neutralize control. Whenever the operation of the environment reveals a structure oriented to capturing vulnerability, obscuring the intelligibility of the relationship, naturalizing functional degradation or imposing asymmetric losses as an ordinary routine of the experience, the analysis must go beyond the rhetoric of technical necessity and inquire into the practical purpose of the arrangement. What matters is not only whether the system can be technically explained, but whether its configuration is legally compatible with good faith, transparency, balance and the protection of the enjoyment legitimately incorporated into the relationship.

Abusive teleology takes on special relevance when exploitation depends not on one major harmful act, but on the repetition of small pressures, small losses and small asymmetries that, accumulated, shape the normality of the environment. This is one of its most important marks. Many exploitative architectures do not produce a spectacular event-harm. They produce ordinary wear, diffuse loss, selective difficulty, progressive obscuring and silent reconfiguration of the experience. Law sometimes tends to underestimate these forms of injury because it was historically better trained to react to delimited events than to operating programs. The parameter proposed here corrects this deficiency by offering a language to capture abusiveness not as an accident, but as a structural vector of supply.

The dogmatic consequence of this is significant. Once abusive teleology is recognized, the legal response must not be limited to the later repair of individual episodes. What opens up is the possibility of protection aimed at correcting the operating regime itself. If the abusiveness lies in the program, it is not enough to treat its isolated effects. It becomes appropriate to consider injunctive relief, reconfiguration of flows, review of selective frictions, duties to give reasons, more symmetrical mechanisms of reversibility, adjustments of informational visibility and other measures capable of reaching architecture as the <1>p. 734</1> continuous source of the problem. The parameter, therefore, broadens the remedial horizon of the IOC regime, because it shifts the focus from the event-harm to the structure that produces and reproduces it.

This broadening, however, does not dissolve rigor. The attribution of abusive teleology cannot arise from vague discomfort with the business model or from intuitive criticism of the existence of monetization, engagement or curation. It requires demonstrating an objectively recognizable functional purpose, revealed by the articulation between governance mechanisms, the vulnerability at stake, the pattern of opacity, the frictions produced and relevant effects on the consumer's practical autonomy and enjoyment. It is this requirement of a chain of reasoning that prevents the trivialization of the category and preserves its institutional usefulness. The parameter does not serve to turn every intense architecture into an unlawful act. It serves to identify when the intensity of design ceases to be merely organizational and comes to structure exploitation incompatible with the limits of the consumer relationship.

For this reason, abusive teleology functions as a closing category of the regime of controllability. Once the object has been qualified, the vulnerability identified, the duties of information and advertising assessed, auditability required and functional equivalence tested, it becomes possible to ask whether the environment as a whole reveals only legitimate governance or whether it already operates as a program of exploitation incorporated into enjoyment itself. When the answer is the latter, architecture ceases to be a backdrop and becomes an unlawful act. It is at this moment that Law ceases to look only at what the platform says or at what it does in isolated episodes, and begins to look at what it builds as a regime.

The effective application of the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption depends on an evidentiary discipline compatible with the contemporary way supply is organized. In platform-governed ecosystems, the asymmetry falls not only on information in the material sense or on abstract economic capacity. It reaches the very terrain of the institutional narrability of the conflict. Whoever controls <1>logs</1>, histories, decision criteria, relevant versions, interface records, moderation flows, alteration parameters and traces of sanction controls, to a large extent, the conditions for legally reconstructing what occurred. Evidence, in this context, is not an element external to the relationship. It is part of the way the relationship is governed. For this reason, the structural opacity of the environment cannot be treated as a <2>p. 735</2> mere neutral fact of technology or as an evidentiary inconvenience to be borne entirely by the consumer.

This point shifts the discussion away from a procedural imaginary still excessively tied to the model of the observable event and the symmetrically accessible document. In many conflicts concerning immaterial objects of consumption, the disputed fact is born, transforms and remains within a technical infrastructure controlled by the supplier. The relevant alteration does not manifest itself as an easily graspable public occurrence. The sanction may be automated or partially automated. The reconfiguration of the object may occur without a sufficient public trail. The essential information may be distributed among internal systems, databases, version records and curation criteria inaccessible to the consumer. In these scenarios, demanding exhaustive evidence from the vulnerable party as if the conditions of production of the litigation were symmetrical means, in practice, rewarding private control of obscurity.

That is why the preservation and disclosure of minimal records take on a central legal status here. Interface trails, histories of relevant versions, essential alteration logs, sanction records, minimal data on automated or assisted decisions, contextual elements of the modulation of enjoyment and other documentary layers indispensable to reconstructing the conflict cannot be understood as business liberality or as a procedural favor granted to the consumer. In environments of governed enjoyment, verifiability forms part of the very duty to shape the relationship legitimately. When the platform administers the experience and at the same time concentrates the traces needed to prove it, the preservation of these elements ceases to be a peripheral question of cooperation and comes to constitute a condition of institutional controllability.

The consequence of this is that a dynamic distribution of the burden of proof is admissible whenever the relevant evidence is structurally under the supplier's technical control. It is not a matter of dramatizing exceptions or of abolishing criteria of procedural rationality. It is a matter of recognizing that formal equality of burdens may operate, in these cases, as a mechanism of material inequality. If the consumer was placed in a scenario of impossible or disproportionately difficult proof because the architecture of the environment concentrates, conceals or volatilizes the relevant elements of the conflict, the evidentiary discipline must react to this asymmetry. Redistributing the burden does not represent anti-technical benevolence. It represents fitting the proceedings to the real design of the consumer relationship.

This parameter thereby avoids one of the most corrosive defenses of structural opacity, which is turning the consumer's lack of access into an absence of proof of the very right claimed. The formula “you did not prove it” becomes institutionally empty when one does not <1>p. 736</1> examine who controlled the conditions for producing, preserving and disclosing what was to be proven. In environments of this nature, the absence of evidence may be less an expression of the weakness of the claim than a result of the supplier's own governance arrangement. Law cannot accept that the platform should simultaneously administer enjoyment, the narrative of the event and the conditions of its verifiability, turning this triple concentration into a self-legitimating procedural advantage.

The evidentiary discipline proposed here is also important because it prevents standards such as open auditability and functional value equivalence from turning into mere conceptual rhetoric. Without a compatible evidentiary regime, these parameters would remain correct in theory, but ineffective in practice. It is not enough to assert that relevant alterations must be intelligible or that enjoyment must remain functionally equivalent. There must be instruments to demonstrate, contest and reconstruct the occurrence of modulations, losses, reconfigurations and sanctions. Evidence, therefore, is not a later and accessory stage of the reasoning. It is a means of efficacy of the regime itself. For this reason, its organization must be conceived from within the dogmatics of the IOC, and not as a secondary problem to be resolved only at the abstract procedural level.

The dynamic distribution of burdens must, in this context, respond to the concrete architecture of the case. The more intense the private concentration of records, the greater the requirement of preservation, delimited disclosure and verifiable justification. The more the reconstruction of the conflict depends on internal governance, the less reasonable it will be to demand from the consumer a detailed demonstration of facts whose documentary and technical support was never within their reach. This does not eliminate the need for plausibility, a chain of argument or delimitation of the disputed object. What it eliminates is the fiction of symmetry in environments whose very structure operates through the asymmetry of meaning and of evidence.

This parameter also has a preventive function. By recognizing that essential records form part of the controllability of the relationship, it encourages the institutional organization of minimal reconstruction trails, discouraging governance models based on the convenient volatilization of the system's memory or on selectively insufficient documentation. The platform that profits from the continuous administration of enjoyment cannot organize this administration in a way that makes unrecoverable, indeterminable or institutionally opaque what will later condition protection. The unjustified failure to preserve or disclose relevant records must not, for this reason, be treated as a mere neutral evidentiary inconvenience. It may authorize presumptions favorable to the consumer and reinforce the attribution of inadequacy to the supply regime.

<1>p. 737</1> At the dogmatic level, the result is clear. In environments of structural opacity, evidence must be read as an internal dimension of the governance of the immaterial object of consumption. The platform does not only supply, alter and sanction. It also conditions the ways in which these operations can be seen, narrated and verified. Recognizing this is a condition for the CDC to retain its efficacy in ecosystems of high technical complexity. Without this recognition, consumer protection runs the risk of remaining formally proclaimed but materially neutralized by architectures that concentrate power not only over enjoyment, but over the very possibility of proving that it was degraded, obscured or abusively governed.

Reconciling the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption with intellectual property rights requires dispelling, from the outset, a recurring confusion. The existence of legally protected exclusivity over content, signs, code, systems, digital assets or platform structures does not amount to an unrestricted legitimation of the way this exclusivity is exercised within the consumer relationship. The protection of intellectual property remains intact on its own plane, but this does not allow its invocation to function as a general clause of immunization against review of adequacy, transparency, loyalty, functional equivalence and protection of enjoyment. In IOC ecosystems, exclusivity explains the legal organization of the environment, but does not neutralize the limits that bear on the way it is exercised.

This point is central because the relationship between intellectual property and continuous digital consumption is usually contaminated by a false alternative. Either one asserts the almost sovereign intangibility of exclusivity, treating any consumer-law interference as an undue threat to the economic architecture of the ecosystem, or one imagines that consumer protection would require reducing intellectual property to a secondary obstacle, devoid of legitimacy of its own. Neither of these positions is adequate. The first turns exclusivity into an unlimited power to govern enjoyment. The second impoverishes the understanding of the environment itself, whose organization frequently depends, legitimately, on exclusive structures of creation, licensing, technical control and economic exploitation. The legal problem lies not in choosing between one pole and the other, but in regulating the coexistence of both under Brazilian constitutional limits.

<1>p. 738</1> From this standpoint, intellectual property must be read in light of the same constitutional rationality that shapes the exercise of property in general. Exclusivity is protected, but its exercise is not an absolute prerogative, detached from the social function, from social interest and from commitment to the constitutional objectives that subordinate private positions to an economic order guided by social justice, consumer protection and national development. This holds with particular force when intellectual property ceases to operate merely as an instrument for protecting creation or innovation and comes to structure environments of captive, continuous and governed enjoyment. In these contexts, exclusivity is not only a legal title over an asset. It is also an infrastructure of private power over access to, permanence in, modulation, updating and contestation of the consumer's experience. The holder of exclusivity consequently retains its economic and technical prerogatives, including the power to organize the ecosystem, protect its assets and preserve internal operating elements. What it does not retain is the possibility of invoking this position to rule out, a priori, review of the way supply is carried out.

Putting this reconciliation into operation runs through the filters already built into the regime. Open auditability is fully compatible with intellectual property because it does not demand full disclosure of trade secrets or total exposure of the technological architecture, but only minimal institutional intelligibility about whatever interferes with enjoyment in a legally relevant way. Functional value equivalence does not deny the prerogative to update, adapt or evolve the environment, but prevents this prerogative from being exercised as a license to hollow out, from within, the legitimately acquired experience. The reconciliation parameter also prevents the debate from being hijacked by an excessively proprietarian grammar, in which every controversy ends up being brought back to the question of who holds the asset or what the abstract extent of the contractual license granted to the user is. The relevant conflict often lies not in the direct violation of a proprietary or authorial position, but in the way exclusive ownership is instrumentalized to govern enjoyment, redistribute risks, concentrate the power of alteration and hinder contestation.

This does not mean that intellectual property is absorbed by the CDC, nor that its regime is reduced to consumer-law logic. It means, rather, a systematic reading compatible with the Constitution. The CDC does not eliminate intellectual property. Intellectual property does not suspend the CDC. What is required is a coexistence governed by criteria of material harmonization, in which exclusivity and consumer protection are read as institutes that <1>p. 739</1> share the same constitutional space and, for that reason, cannot be interpreted as cancelling each other out. In ecosystems of governed enjoyment, this harmonization requires recognizing that the exercise of exclusivity becomes legally more intense, more structural and more consequential for the consumer's experience. Precisely for that reason, it also becomes more subject to review as to its effects.

The parameter, therefore, affirms a thesis that is simple in its formulation and severe in its consequences. Intellectual property protects the ecosystem, but does not absolve its governance. Where there is conflict between the concrete way exclusivity is exercised and the duties of loyalty, transparency, equivalence and restoration proper to the IOC regime, the solution must be sought through the functional reconciliation of the institutes, under the primacy of Brazilian constitutional limits and of the social function that shapes the legitimate use of proprietary positions. This is how exclusivity remains protected without turning into private sovereignty over the consumption experience.
